title: Saturday of the Thirty-first Week in Ordinary Time
meditation: Dear brothers and sisters in Christ,

Today, Saint Paul helps us discover the power of trusting in God. When a person truly places his trust in Christ, he discovers within himself a strength that goes beyond his own abilities. With Christ, we can face difficulties, overcome our weaknesses and accomplish great things. Our strength does not come merely from our talents or personal efforts, but above all from our union with the Lord. That is why we should never lose heart in the face of difficulties, because whoever walks with Christ is never abandoned.

However, one of the greatest victories we are called to achieve in life is the victory of self-control. We live in a world full of temptations, which sometimes take very ordinary forms: gluttony, the excessive pursuit of pleasure, lack of discipline, and dishonesty in the management of money. Jesus particularly warns us against the misuse of wealth and the danger of becoming slaves to money. Indeed, it is not enough to be capable of accomplishing great things; we must also learn to control our desires, remain honest in our actions and keep our hearts free from attachment to worldly possessions. The true greatness of a Christian is also revealed in the ability to resist evil, even when nobody is watching.

Dear brothers and sisters, let us ask the Lord to give us the strength to live with this inner freedom. May our trust in Christ help us overcome our weaknesses and prevent us from being dominated by our appetites, personal interests or the attraction of money. Let us learn to be faithful in little things, because it is often through the ordinary actions of our daily lives that the quality of our Christian life is revealed. Let us not seek only to accomplish great things with Christ; let us above all strive to remain faithful to him in the little things of everyday life.
Father Dieudonné MANIRAGUHA

title: Friday of the Thirty-first Week in Ordinary Time - Our Citizenship Is in Heaven
meditation: Dear brothers and sisters in Christ,

Saint Paul reminds us of a fundamental truth of our faith: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil 3:20). These words invite us never to lose sight of our true identity and our ultimate destination. Certainly, we live in this world, where we have responsibilities, projects and commitments, but we must never forget that our permanent home is with God. That is why we are called to live, even now, as citizens of heaven, allowing our choices, words and actions to be guided by the values of the Gospel. Preparing ourselves to enter our heavenly homeland means learning every day to love more deeply, to forgive, to serve others and to remain faithful to the Lord.

In today's Gospel (Lk 16:1-8), Jesus surprises us by praising the dishonest steward, not because of his dishonesty, but because of his resourcefulness and foresight. He knew how to take initiatives and use his intelligence to prepare for the future. In this way, Jesus invites us, too, to demonstrate creativity, discernment and determination in our spiritual journey. If people of this world are capable of using so much ingenuity to secure their earthly interests, how much more should the disciples of Christ put their intelligence, talents and resources at the service of God's Kingdom! Let us therefore not be passive in our faith. Rather, let us seek concrete ways of doing good, supporting others and making fruitful use of the gifts God has entrusted to us.

In this regard, the technological advances taking place in our world today, about which Pope Leo XIV invites us to reflect, particularly in his teaching on human dignity and technological progress, also offer us an opportunity to renew our Christian commitment. Technology is neither an end in itself nor a threat that must automatically be rejected; it can become a valuable instrument at the service of the Gospel, fraternity and human development, provided that it is used wisely and responsibly. Let us therefore put the possibilities of our time at the service of what is good, rather than allowing ourselves to become enslaved by them. The real question is not simply how far technological progress can take us in this world, but rather how we can use it to prepare ourselves better for our encounter with God. May all our initiatives, knowledge and talents help us draw closer to our heavenly homeland, where the Lord awaits us. Amen.
Father Dieudonné MANIRAGUHA

title: Thursday of the Thirty-first Week in Ordinary Time
meditation: Dear brothers and sisters in Christ, detachment and renunciation occupy an essential place in the life of every believer who desires to follow the Lord faithfully. Drawing from his own experience, Saint Paul invites us to consider the advantages and riches of this world as losses, even as rubbish, compared with the incomparable value of knowing Christ and living in communion with Him (Phil 3:7-8). Indeed, following Christ requires us to make choices, to renounce whatever separates us from God, and to recognize that nothing can compare with the joy of belonging to Him.

This detachment does not mean despising life or rejecting the gifts God has given us. Rather, it means having an inner freedom that prevents us from becoming slaves to worldly possessions and pleasures. It gives us the strength to resist sin, overcome our weaknesses and maintain a simple heart, always available and fully devoted to our Divine Master. Those who truly attach themselves to Christ gradually learn to detach themselves from everything that might take His place in their hearts.

Therefore, dear young people, both young and old, let us have the courage to put this Gospel teaching into practice. Let us learn to reject everything that is displeasing in the eyes of God and develop a genuine hatred for sin in all its forms. Let us not be carried away by passing pleasures or the temporary riches of this world. Instead, let us ask the Lord for a free and generous heart, ready to leave everything behind interiorly in order to follow Him more faithfully, for Christ Himself is the greatest treasure of our lives.
Father Dieudonné MANIRAGUHA

title: Memorial of Saint Charles Borromeo, Bishop
meditation: Dear brothers and sisters in Christ,

'Work out your salvation with fear and trembling,' Saint Paul exhorts us (Phil 2:12). Saint Augustine beautifully expresses this truth when he says: “God, who created us without us, will not save us without our cooperation.” These words remind us that salvation is first and foremost a free gift from God, but it also calls for our personal cooperation. God offers us His grace and invites us to respond through a life of faith, fidelity and commitment. We must therefore not remain passive, waiting for God to do everything for us, but rather allow ourselves to be transformed by His love and take our spiritual journey seriously.

That is why we must ask the Lord for the grace to work out our salvation each day through small acts of renunciation, as the Gospel invites us to do. Renouncing our pride, bad habits, disordered attachments and everything that separates us from God are concrete ways of showing our desire to follow Him. The journey towards salvation sometimes demands sacrifices, but no renunciation made out of love for God is ever in vain. May the Lord give us the courage not to be discouraged by the demands of the Gospel, but to follow Him faithfully each day, confident that His grace goes before us, accompanies us and ultimately leads us to eternal life.
Father Dieudonné MANIRAGUHA

title: Tuesday of the Thirty-First Week in Ordinary Time
meditation: Today, the Word of God invites us to remain ever open and ready to respond to God's call.

In our daily lives, it is all too easy to become caught up in numerous activities, some of which may seem indispensable, yet gradually lead us to overlook what is most essential: our life with God. This is often reflected in our relationship with Him, where our attachment to material possessions, money, and even family ties can sometimes become obstacles to our spiritual growth and Christian journey.

The twofold invitation in today's Gospel refers first to God's call to Israel and then to His invitation extended to all the nations. The Acts of the Apostles recounts this transition from Israel to the Gentiles, a decisive moment in the history of the Church, reminding us that God's salvation is intended for all humanity, without exception.

Dear brothers and sisters, the Lord invites us to walk with Him. He comes to meet us in great humility, as the first reading reminds us, so that He may become one of us and share in our human condition.
Let us therefore give Him our response and avoid every form of refusal. Indeed, the reasons that lead us to postpone or turn down God's invitations are not always beneficial to our lives.
May we never allow our earthly concerns to prevent us from welcoming the Lord into our hearts.
Wishing you all a blessed day!
Father Dieudonné MANIRAGUHA

title: Commemoration of all departed souls
meditation: My dear brothers and sisters,

On this day, when the Church raises her prayers to God for all the faithful departed, the Word of God invites us to turn our gaze towards Christ, the Lord of life, who calls all those who believe in him to share in the resurrection. Today's Gospel reminds us of a fundamental truth of our faith: we were not created for death, but for eternal life. God created us out of love and calls us to live forever in his presence. By giving himself to us as food in his Body and Blood, Christ has left us the pledge of this imperishable life: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him on the last day” (Jn 6:54).

The Solemnity of All Saints, which we celebrated yesterday, and today's Commemoration of All the Faithful Departed invite us to contemplate the profound mystery of the communion of the Church. Indeed, the Church is not limited to the community of believers who are still making their earthly pilgrimage. She also embraces those who, having completed their journey on earth, already enjoy the glory of heaven, as well as those who are still undergoing purification in preparation for the fullness of communion with God. This is what the Church's tradition describes as the three states of the one Church: the Church Triumphant, made up of the saints and the blessed who enjoy the glory of heaven; the Church Suffering, consisting of those who are still undergoing purification in the hope of entering fully into the presence of God; and the Church Militant, to which we still belong as we journey through this earthly life. These are three states of one and the same Church, united in Christ and destined to be gathered together in the fullness of the Kingdom of God.

In this perspective, the Commemoration of the Faithful Departed is not a celebration dominated by sadness or fear of death. Above all, it is a celebration of Christian hope. It invites us not to remain fixed on the tomb, but to raise our eyes towards the One who passed through death and conquered it once and for all: Jesus Christ, the firstborn from the dead (Col 1:18). With Saint Paul, we can therefore proclaim: “Death, where is your victory? Death, where is your sting?” (1 Cor 15:55). Death no longer has the final word, because the risen Christ has opened for us the way to eternal life. Through the sacraments, and especially through the Eucharist, he already communicates this new life to us and gives us the medicine of immortality, gradually drawing us into his own victory over death.

This is why we believe that our departed brothers and sisters have not been annihilated. Those who have left us in faith and hope have not fallen into nothingness; their lives remain in the hands of God. Death has not destroyed their existence; rather, it has marked their passage towards the encounter with the Lord to which we are all called. Although we do not know the particular path of purification of each soul, we know that God's mercy is infinitely greater than our human limitations. This is why the Church prays for her departed children, trusting in the power of divine mercy, which can lead them into the fullness of God's light.

All the acts of piety that we undertake on this day — our prayers, visits to cemeteries, acts of charity and, above all, the celebration of the Holy Eucharist — are therefore rooted in faith and love. We offer them for our departed brothers and sisters, asking the Lord, in his infinite goodness, to complete in them the work of purification and welcome them into the communion of saints. By praying for them, we also proclaim that the bonds of love are not broken by death and that our communion in Christ remains stronger than physical separation.

My dear brothers and sisters, on this day of remembrance, let us entrust all our departed loved ones to the loving tenderness of the Father. Let us pray for those whom we have loved, those whose memory we cherish, but also for all those who died in solitude, in obscurity, or without anyone to remember them in prayer. And as we intercede for them, let us renew our own hope: one day, we too shall cross the threshold of death and stand before the Lord. May this prospect encourage us to live now in faith, charity and fidelity to the Gospel.
Lord, grant eternal rest to all our departed brothers and sisters. May your perpetual light shine upon them, and may your mercy lead them into the joy of your Kingdom. May they rest in peace. Amen.
Father Dieudonné MANIRAGUHA

title: As he who called you is holy, be holy yourselves in all your conduct; for it is written: ‘You shall be holy, for I am holy.’” (1 Peter 1:15–16)- Solemnity of All Saints
meditation: Dear brothers and sisters in Christ, As we celebrate the Solemnity of All Saints today, allow me to begin this meditation with these words of exhortation from the Apostle Peter, who reminds us that holiness is the ultimate goal of the entire Christian life.

The saints whom we commemorate today were men and women of their own time. Like us, they experienced the joys and trials of human existence; like us, they believed in God and walked in faith. However, they left us a precious testimony through their lives, which remains a light and an encouragement on our journey towards God.

They form that vast and countless multitude presented to us in today's first reading. They now enjoy the fullness of happiness because they live in God's presence and are filled with His blessings. Indeed, the supreme joy of the saints consists in the beatific vision of God, in that eternal contemplation of the One who is the source of all love and happiness. Conversely, the greatest suffering of the damned consists precisely in being deprived forever of God's presence.

But we, dear brothers and sisters, are filled with firm hope: the hope that one day we shall behold the face of God and share in eternal happiness with all the saints who have gone before us. Saint John reminds us of this in the second reading: we are already children of God, although what we shall become has not yet been fully revealed. Nevertheless, we know that when Christ appears, we shall be like Him, because we shall see Him as He really is.

In the light of this hope, and in response to the invitation of the eight Beatitudes proclaimed in today's Gospel, Let us strive, dear brothers and sisters, to make the Gospel the true light of our lives. Holiness is not an ideal reserved for a few extraordinary people; it is a vocation addressed to each and every one of us. It is built day by day through our choices, our words, our attitudes and, above all, through the way we love God and our neighbour.

May our actions, therefore, reflect the charity of Christ, so that at the end of our earthly pilgrimage, the Lord may address these words of promise to us: “Come, you who are blessed by my Father; inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink; I was naked and you clothed me…” (Matthew 25:34–36).

May our patron saints intercede for us, accompany us through their prayers, and obtain for us the grace to follow Christ faithfully, until the day when we shall be united with them in the glory of the Kingdom of Heaven.
A blessed and holy Feast of All Saints to everyone!
